title: Comparison of Polarized Versus Other Types of Endurance Training Intensity Distribution on Athletes’ Endurance Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
authors: Silva Oliveira P; Boppre G; Fonseca H
key: Polarized training showed a small advantage for VO2peak, particularly in highly trained athletes and interventions under 12 weeks, but was not superior for time trial, time-to-exhaustion, or power/speed at VT2/LT2.
app: Do not hard-code an 80/20 polarized dogma. Offer polarized and pyramidal distributions as evidence-supported templates and select by athlete level, phase, event and response.

title: Training Periodization, Intensity Distribution, and Volume in Trained Cyclists: A Systematic Review
authors: Galán-Rioja MA; Gonzalez-Ravé JM; González-Mohíno F; Seiler S
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
key: Cycling studies use multiple periodization and intensity-distribution models; the literature does not establish one universally superior model across contexts.
app: Make periodization configurable. Bias toward high low-intensity volume with targeted quality rather than claiming a single optimal distribution.

title: The proportional distribution of training by elite endurance athletes at different intensities during different phases of the season
authors: Sperlich B; Matzka M; Holmberg HC
journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
key: Across reported elite-athlete training distributions, pyramidal and polarized patterns were both common and varied by sport and phase of season.
app: Allow intensity distribution to evolve across a season: pyramidal base/build is common; more polarized patterns may emerge in some phases.

title: Training Session Models in Endurance Sports: A Norwegian Perspective on Best Practice Recommendations
authors: Tønnessen E; Sandbakk Ø; Sandbakk SB; Seiler S; Haugen T
population: 12 world-leading Norwegian endurance coaches across Olympic endurance sports
key: Successful endurance programmes feature high volumes of low intensity work and controlled, repeatable interval sessions that are often less exhaustive than research intervention protocols.
app: Default hard sessions should usually finish with reserve rather than failure. Protect repeatability and consistency over chasing maximal session scores.

title: What is Best Practice for Training Intensity and Duration Distribution in Endurance Athletes?
authors: Seiler S
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
key: A large proportion of successful endurance training is performed at low intensity, with a smaller but important dose of high intensity work.
app: Use low-intensity volume as the foundation and constrain high-intensity frequency to what the athlete can absorb.

title: Polarized training has greater impact on key endurance variables than threshold, high intensity, or high volume training
authors: Stöggl T; Sperlich B
key: In this intervention, a polarized programme produced strong improvements in several endurance outcomes compared with alternative distributions.
app: Use as supportive—not definitive—evidence for polarized blocks, especially when an athlete is stagnating under threshold-heavy training.

title: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Wang Z; Wang Y; Gao W; Zhong Y
key: Tapering improves time-trial/time-to-exhaustion performance. The best-supported approach reduces volume about 41–60%, keeps intensity and frequency, and lasts up to 21 days.
app: For priority events, create 7–14 day default tapers (extend toward 21 days for large accumulated load) with ~40–60% volume reduction while retaining short intensity exposures.

title: Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis
authors: Bosquet L; Montpetit J; Arvisais D; Mujika I
key: Classic taper meta-analysis supports approximately two weeks of tapering with a substantial progressive reduction in volume while intensity is maintained.
app: Use as foundational taper logic and cross-check with newer Wang 2023 synthesis.

title: Time spent at or near V̇O₂max during high-intensity interval training - a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Schoenmakers P; Murray K; White J; Matta G; Bossi AH
journal: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
key: Long intervals of at least ~2 minutes generally generate more accumulated time near VO2max than short/moderate intervals; variable-intensity work can increase time near VO2max.
app: When the goal is VO2 stimulus, prioritize repeatable 2–5 minute intervals or carefully designed variable intervals rather than treating any hard workout as equivalent.

title: Meta-analyses of the effects of high-intensity interval training in elite athletes—part I: mean effects on various performance measures
authors: Wiesinger HP; Stöggl TL; Haller N; et al.
key: HIIT can improve multiple performance measures even in highly trained athletes; more aerobic long-interval formats appear especially useful for VO2max.
app: Scale expected gains by athlete calibre; advanced riders need highly targeted HIIT rather than simply more intensity.

title: High-Intensity Interval Training, Solutions to the Programming Puzzle: Part I: Cardiopulmonary Emphasis
authors: Buchheit M; Laursen PB
key: HIIT responses are determined by multiple variables including work duration, intensity, recovery duration, recovery intensity and modality.
app: Model interval workouts as a parameter set, not a single label. Match work/recovery configuration to the targeted physiological response.

title: High-Intensity Interval Training, Solutions to the Programming Puzzle: Part II: Anaerobic Energy, Neuromuscular Load and Practical Applications
authors: Buchheit M; Laursen PB
key: Different HIIT formats alter anaerobic contribution, neuromuscular load and recovery cost.
app: Track session purpose and fatigue cost separately. Two sessions with similar TSS can impose very different neuromuscular and metabolic stress.

title: Short intervals induce superior training adaptations compared with long intervals in cyclists – an effort-matched approach
authors: Rønnestad BR; Hansen J; Vegge G; Tønnessen E; Slettaløkken G
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
key: In this study, short work/rest intervals produced strong adaptations compared with longer interval sessions under the tested design.
app: Keep 30/15-style microintervals as an alternative VO2 format, especially for riders who struggle to sustain long intervals.

title: Number of Sprint Repetitions in a Sprint Interval Training Session Does Not Moderate Improvements in V̇O₂max With Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Hutchinson M; Kinghorn DJ; Hall ECR; et al.
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
key: Sprint interval training improved VO2max substantially across studies, but doing more sprint repetitions per session did not explain larger improvements.
app: If prescribing SIT, avoid assuming more repetitions are better. Use the minimum effective, tolerable dose and account for high fatigue and adherence cost.

title: Power profiling and the power-duration relationship in cycling: a narrative review
authors: Leo P; Spragg J; Podlogar T; Lawley JS; Mujika I
key: Structured multi-duration testing and power-duration modelling provide a richer cyclist fingerprint than single-effort metrics; the authors recommend avoiding single-effort prediction trials such as FTP as the sole model.
app: Build a power-duration curve from multiple efforts and recent ride data. Use FTP as a convenient field metric, not the only anchor for zones or progression.

title: What is known about the FTP20 test related to cycling? A scoping review
authors: Mackey J; Horner K
key: FTP20 is generally reliable but shows limits of agreement with physiological threshold markers large enough that the measures should not be treated as interchangeable.
app: Label FTP as an estimate/field performance metric. Never claim that 95% of 20-min power precisely equals lactate threshold or maximal metabolic steady state for every rider.

title: Durability as an index of endurance exercise performance: Methodological considerations
authors: Hunter B; Maunder E; Jones AM; Gallo G; Muniz-Pumares D
key: Durability is the resilience of physiological/performance variables to deterioration during or after prolonged exercise. Results are strongly influenced by the fatiguing protocol, nutrition and environment.
app: Track power/HR/decoupling and changes in short-to-medium duration power after accumulated work. Standardize pre-test fuelling and conditions before comparing durability scores.

title: Durability as an independent parameter of endurance performance in cycling
authors: Barsumyan A; Soost C; Shyla R; et al.
journal: BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation
key: After 1000 kJ of prior work, 5- and 20-min power fell by about 10% on average; durability was not clearly related to VO2max or relative FTP.
app: Treat durability as a separate performance dimension. Include “fresh vs fatigued power” tests for long-event athletes rather than assuming a high FTP means strong late-race performance.

title: Heavy strength training effects on physiological determinants of endurance cyclist performance: a systematic review with meta-analysis
authors: Llanos-Lagos C; Ramirez-Campillo R; Sáez de Villarreal E
key: Heavy strength training (≥80% 1RM) improved cycling efficiency, anaerobic power and cycling performance, without clear effects on VO2max. Benefits appear after sufficient duration/dose.
app: For healthy riders, use 2 strength sessions/week in development blocks, centred on heavy lower-body compound lifts; maintain with ~1 session/week when cycling intensity/competition rises.

title: Optimizing strength training for running and cycling endurance performance: A review
authors: Rønnestad BR; Mujika I
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
key: Heavy strength training can improve endurance performance determinants through neuromuscular and efficiency-related mechanisms, with appropriate integration into endurance training.
app: Prioritize maximal strength and neural quality over bodybuilding-style fatigue. Use long rests and avoid routine lifting to failure.

title: Strength training improves performance and pedaling characteristics in elite cyclists
authors: Rønnestad BR; Hansen J; Hollan I; Ellefsen S
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
key: Long-term heavy strength training improved several cycling performance determinants and performance outcomes in well-trained cyclists.
app: Strength gains need months, not a token 2–3 week block. Make strength a year-round component with development and maintenance phases.

title: Compatibility of Concurrent Aerobic and Strength Training for Skeletal Muscle Size and Function: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Schumann M; Feuerbacher JF; Sünkeler M; et al.
directness: General concurrent training; cycling subgroup assessed
key: Concurrent endurance + strength generally does not compromise hypertrophy or maximal strength, but explosive strength gains can be attenuated, especially when both are performed in the same session.
app: Separate key strength and key endurance sessions by several hours or different days when possible. If same day, order by the primary adaptation goal and keep the second session low-cost.

title: Chronic Effects of Static Stretching Exercises on Muscle Strength and Power in Healthy Individuals Across the Lifespan: A Systematic Review with Multi-level Meta-analysis
authors: Arntz F; Markov A; Behm DG; et al.
key: Long-term static stretching improves flexibility and may produce trivial-to-small positive strength/power effects; it is not inherently harmful when programmed appropriately.
app: Use stretching mainly for range of motion and comfort goals. Do not market it as a major cycling-performance intervention.

title: Application of mobility training methods in sporting populations: A systematic review of performance adaptations
authors: Skopal LK; Drinkwater EJ; Behm DG
key: Mobility interventions can improve range of motion and selected physical-performance measures, but methods and outcomes vary.
app: Offer short mobility routines based on measured restriction or rider comfort, not mandatory generic mobility volume for everyone.

title: Effect of yoga on selected performance metrics and mental health of track and field athletes: A systematic review
authors: Multiple authors
journal: Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies
key: Yoga appears useful for flexibility, balance and some wellbeing/performance measures, but direct cycling-performance evidence remains sparse and study quality is limited.
app: Position yoga as an optional adjunct for mobility, balance, breathing/relaxation and adherence—not a substitute for cycling or strength training.

title: Effectiveness of Recovery Strategies After Training and Competition in Endurance Athletes: An Umbrella Review
authors: Li S; Kempe M; Brink M; et al.
key: No recovery modality is consistently superior across outcomes. Some modalities may help particular soreness/perception outcomes, but effects on subsequent performance are inconsistent.
app: Prioritize sleep, nutrition, rest and load management. Treat massage, compression, cold water and similar tools as optional, context-dependent add-ons.

title: Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations
authors: Walsh NP; Halson SL; Sargent C; et al.
key: Athletes have individual sleep needs and are vulnerable to sleep restriction. Sleep extension, naps and sleep-hygiene strategies can be useful when individualized.
app: Track sleep opportunity and perceived sleep quality, not just wearable stages. Flag repeated short sleep and adjust demanding sessions where performance/readiness is clearly impaired.

title: Monitoring Athlete Training Loads: Consensus Statement
authors: Bourdon PC; Cardinale M; Murray A; et al.
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
key: Training-load monitoring should combine internal and external load measures and be interpreted in context; there is no single best metric.
app: Combine power/duration (external load), session RPE/HR (internal load), and subjective state. Avoid automated decisions based on CTL, TSS, HRV or resting HR alone.

title: Heart Rate Variability-Guided Training for Enhancing Cardiac-Vagal Modulation, Aerobic Fitness, and Endurance Performance: A Methodological Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
authors: Manresa-Rocamora A; Sarabia JM; Javaloyes A; et al.
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
key: HRV-guided training can improve some aerobic/physiological outcomes and may reduce non-response, but performance advantages are modest/inconsistent and protocols differ.
app: Use HRV as one readiness input with individualized baselines and trends. Never cancel or prescribe intensity solely from one morning reading.

title: Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of the overtraining syndrome: joint consensus statement of the ECSS and ACSM
authors: Meeusen R; Duclos M; Foster C; et al.
key: Functional overreaching, non-functional overreaching and overtraining syndrome are clinically distinct concepts; persistent performance decline requires exclusion of illness and other causes.
app: Do not diagnose overtraining from an app. Escalate persistent unexplained performance decline, fatigue, mood/sleep disturbance or illness symptoms to a qualified clinician.

title: Nutrition and Athletic Performance
authors: Thomas DT; Erdman KA; Burke LM
journal: Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics / ACSM joint position
key: Energy, carbohydrate, protein, fluid and micronutrient intake should be periodized to support training demands and recovery.
app: Tie fuelling prompts to session duration/intensity and daily training load rather than giving one fixed diet prescription.

title: New Horizons in Carbohydrate Research and Application for Endurance Athletes
authors: Podlogar T; Wallis GA
key: Carbohydrate remains central to prolonged/high-intensity endurance performance. Multiple-transportable carbohydrate strategies enable high exogenous oxidation; intakes above traditional 90 g/h are an emerging advanced option for some athletes/events.
app: Use tiered fuelling: lower amounts for short/easy rides; ~60–90 g/h for prolonged demanding rides; >90 g/h only as an advanced, practiced gut-training strategy rather than a universal target.

title: Protein Nutrition for Endurance Athletes: A Metabolic Focus on Promoting Recovery and Training Adaptation
authors: Witard OC; Hearris M; Morgan PT
key: Endurance athletes may benefit from protein intakes toward the upper end of traditional sports recommendations, especially under heavy load, recovery or low-carbohydrate availability.
app: Use a broad evidence-aware protein range rather than a rigid value; distribute protein across meals and prioritize sufficient total energy/carbohydrate first.

title: 2023 International Olympic Committee’s consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)
authors: Mountjoy M; Ackerman KE; Bailey DM; et al.
key: Problematic low energy availability can impair health and performance in athletes of all sexes; low carbohydrate availability can contribute to risk.
app: Never encourage chronic under-fuelling for weight loss or “train low” without safeguards. Add RED-S warning flags and refer persistent symptoms to sports medicine/dietetic professionals.

title: International society of sports nutrition position stand: caffeine and exercise performance
authors: Guest NS; VanDusseldorp TA; Nelson MT; et al.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
key: Caffeine can improve endurance and other performance outcomes for many athletes; common effective doses are around 3–6 mg/kg, with some benefit at lower doses and greater side-effect risk at high doses.
app: If included, make caffeine optional, individualized and bounded by sleep, tolerance, medical considerations and competition rules. Do not normalize high dosing.

title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement
authors: Sawka MN; Burke LM; Eichner ER; et al.
key: Hydration strategies should aim to avoid excessive dehydration and overdrinking, with individual sweat rates and environmental demands considered.
app: Estimate sweat rate from pre/post body mass when practical. Never prescribe drinking that causes body-mass gain during exercise; individualize fluid/sodium prompts by conditions and tolerance.

title: The Influence of Drinking Fluid on Endurance Cycling Performance: A Meta-Analysis
authors: Holland JJ; Skinner TL; Irwin CG; Leveritt MD; Goulet EDB
key: The effect of drinking during cycling is duration- and intensity-dependent; fluid helped longer moderate-intensity cycling in the included studies but could impose a performance cost in shorter high-intensity trials.
app: Individualize fluid intake by duration, intensity, heat and tolerance rather than mandating maximal replacement. Avoid both excessive dehydration and overdrinking.

title: Consensus recommendations on training and competing in the heat
authors: Racinais S; Alonso JM; Coutts AJ; et al.
key: Heat acclimation is an effective preparation strategy; repeated heat exposures over roughly 1–2 weeks produce substantial cardiovascular and thermoregulatory adaptation.
app: For hot-event preparation, offer a heat-acclimation module using progressive, controlled exposure, hydration monitoring and conservative safety limits.

title: Cardiorespiratory and metabolic consequences of detraining in endurance athletes
authors: Barbieri A; Fuk A; Gallo G; et al.
key: Training cessation reduces cardiorespiratory and metabolic adaptations; partial training can attenuate losses, while longer cessation causes broader decline.
app: After meaningful time off, automatically reduce prior training targets and rebuild through a re-entry block rather than resuming historical load/FTP workouts unchanged.

title: Factors associated with overuse injury in cyclists: A systematic review
authors: Multiple authors
journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
key: Evidence linking many specific bike/body-fit measures to overuse injury is weak; previous symptoms and load-related factors have more consistent support than simplistic fit rules.
app: Do not diagnose pain from saddle height/knee angle formulas. Use load change and symptom history as core flags, then recommend qualified bike-fit/clinical assessment where needed.

title: Defining Training and Performance Caliber: A Participant Classification Framework
authors: McKay AKA; Stellingwerff T; Smith ES; et al.
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
key: A six-tier framework distinguishes sedentary through world-class participants, addressing inconsistent use of labels such as “elite”.
app: Store an athlete-calibre tag on every evidence rule so findings from untrained participants are not automatically applied to national/elite riders.

title: The Effects of Menstrual Cycle Phase on Exercise Performance in Eumenorrheic Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: McNulty KL; Elliott-Sale KJ; Dolan E; et al.
key: Average performance differences across menstrual-cycle phases were trivial, with large between-study variation and low-quality evidence limiting phase-based prescriptions.
app: Do not auto-periodize training by predicted cycle phase. Allow symptom tracking and individualized adaptation where repeated personal patterns exist.

title: Consensus Statements—Optimizing Performance of the Elite Athlete (female-athlete section)
authors: International expert consensus group
key: Current evidence is insufficient to prescribe training, nutrition or injury-prevention changes by menstrual phase; athlete-specific symptoms and clinically valid information should guide adjustments.
app: Treat cycle tracking as context, not a deterministic training engine.

title: Endurance exercise performance: the physiology of champions
authors: Joyner MJ; Coyle EF
key: Endurance performance can be understood through interacting determinants including VO2max, sustainable fraction/threshold and economy/efficiency, shaped by training and morphology.
app: Model performance as multidimensional. A rider can improve through VO2max, threshold/critical power, efficiency, anaerobic capacity and durability—not FTP alone.

title: The Scientific Basis for High-Intensity Interval Training: Optimising Training Programmes and Maximising Performance in Highly Trained Endurance Athletes
authors: Laursen PB; Jenkins DG
key: HIIT is a potent tool for trained endurance athletes but must be carefully dosed and integrated with lower-intensity work.
app: Do not turn the app into a HIIT generator. High-intensity sessions are a minority tool inside a sustainable programme.

title: Effects of different interval-training programs on cycling time-trial performance
authors: Stepto NK; Hawley JA; Dennis SC; Hopkins WG
key: Different high-intensity interval formats can improve time-trial performance, reinforcing the importance of matching interval design to the athlete and target.
app: Maintain a library of distinct interval types rather than one generic VO2 workout.

title: A new approach to monitoring exercise training
authors: Foster C; Florhaug JA; Franklin J; et al.
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
key: Session-RPE provides a simple, low-cost measure of internal training load that can complement objective workload.
app: Collect session RPE after every ride/strength session. It remains valuable even when power, HR and wearable data are available.
